newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analyst reduces nickel price forecast for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Analyst reduces nickel price forecast for 1997.

text.p: Analysts CRU International Ltd reduced its forecast for the average nickel price in 1997 to $3.50 per lb at best from $3.50-3.55 earlier this month, CRU nickel specialist Fidelis Madavo said on Wednesday.
"Nickel has become quite disappointing, the main reason being there is a lot more scrap available than previously thought," he told Reuters during the Metal Bulletin stainless steel conference here.
"Higher nickel prices this year have attracted a lot of scrap material from the Commonwealth of Independent States," Madavo said.
He also cited an anticipated weakening in stainless steel demand in the second half of 1997, which should reduce demand for nickel, two thirds of which goes into stainless steel.
CRU's early June forecast was already down from the $3.60 initially projected for 1997, but it was still up from around $3.40 seen in 1996.
Higher year-on-year price projections for nickel are rooted in a strong recovery in stainless output and demand, but Madavo said the market was now at a crossroads.
"Stainless steel sales have gone well so far but many distributors are now holding more stainlesss products than normal," he said.
"Some orders are being cancelled and mills may reduce production in the second half of 1997."
Madavo also said news that producer Inco of Canada would resume talks with striking unions was bearish for the nickel price.
Russia's Norilsk Nickel metals group NKEL.RTS, by contrast, might not be able to increase production in 1997 at the rate it has projected.
Madavo cited gas supply problems and financial problems at the works, which accounts for around 85 percent of Russian output and aims to become the world's number one nickel supplier.
"They are not going to achieve the high production they were talking about...I never believed they could do 213,000 tonnes (envisaged by Norilsk after 177,185 in 1996)," Madavo said.
Further ahead, the analyst believed a nickel price peak forecast by CRU for 1998 might be slightly postponed.

A post-1998 slide on the emergence of new nickel mining projects might not happen if there were further delays to the Voisey's Bay project in Labrador, Canada, and if progress in some Australian projects failed to materialise.
